The greatest part of a brokerage account is the flexibility. You can -buy when you want and however much you want -sell when you want and however much you want -hold however long you want But when you do sell, you have to pay taxes on your gains 1)you pay capital gains taxes (paying taxes on the money you make from your stock, etf, mutual fund) 2)you can deduct your taxes if you have LOST money on your investments too up to a certain amount a year (look up tax loss harvesting and/or wash sales if you really curious) You either pay  1) long-term capital gains if you’ve had the investment for over a year (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on your income) Or  2) short-term capital gains taxes if you’ve had the investment for less than a year (up to 35% depending on your income) How to use the brokerage account: - After people have maxed out their 401k/403b/457b, Trad/Roth IRA, HSA, they typically invest whatever money they have left over into a brokerage account. -I have some friends who are using their brokerage accounts to fund their sabbatical and to pay off their graduate tuition!! Replying to @PlasticThottle 📈 SOME LESS COMMONLY TALKED ABOUT BONDs: 🌟 Corporate bonds, meaning you're lending to companies: LQD is investment grade corporate, VCIT is intermediate corporate, VCSH is short-term corporate. 🌟 Treasuries, lending to the US government: VGIT for intermediate, VGSH for short-term, TLT for long-term, SGOV for very short-term treasury bills. TIP and VTIP are inflation-protected. 🌟 Municipal bonds, lending to states and cities, and the interest is usually federal tax free: VTEB, MUB. 🌟 High yield, sometimes called junk bonds, meaning riskier companies paying more: HYG, JNK. why not just buy one company's bonds???? you can buy Apple or Microsoft bonds directly, but they usually trade in $1,000 or $2,000 minimums and the pricing is a bit unclear for regular investors. LQD holds thousands of corporate bonds at once. it’s the same logic as index funds versus single stocks. the 100% stocks debate: there's research showing a 90/10 portfolio gives up very little in long-run return compared to 100% stocks while cutting the worst year meaningfully. there's also recent research arguing the opposite, that all stocks split between US and international beats a target date fund over a lifetime. so it's a lil up in the air, and the practical takeaway is that the return difference is small either way. the real question is whether you'd stay invested through a 40% drop. 👀👀👀 how bonds actually behave in your 401k: most employer plans have a bond fund in the investment menu, often just called "bond index" or "stable value." those are two different things. stable value is closer to cash.  #bonds #bondinvesting #investingforbeginners #PersonalFinance #assetallocation

If you don’t understand the difference between stocks and bonds… you’re basically investing blind 👀 Let’s break it down simply: 📈 Stocks = Ownership When you buy a stock, you own a piece of a company.  That means: • Your money can grow faster • You can earn dividends • BUT… prices can go up and down (sometimes fast) 💰 Bonds = Lending When you buy a bond, you’re loaning money to a company or the government.  That means: • You get paid interest • More stable than stocks • BUT usually lower returns over time 💡 So why does this matter? Because your mix of stocks vs. bonds determines: ➡️ How fast your money can grow ➡️ How much risk you’re taking ➡️ How you handle market drops Example:  • More stocks = higher growth, more ups & downs  • More bonds = more stability, slower growth ⚖️ This is called your asset allocation, and it’s one of the MOST important decisions you’ll make when investing. 🚨 Mistake people make: Going all in on one without understanding why The goal isn’t picking one… It’s building the right balance for YOUR life, timeline, and risk tolerance. caption: Systematic vs. Unsystematic Risk — explained simply. Systematic risk = risk that affects the entire market  Think: inflation, interest rates, recessions, or major economic events. Unsystematic risk = risk specific to one company or industry  Think: a lawsuit, bad earnings report, management problems, or a product failure. The key difference: Diversification can reduce unsystematic risk, but it can’t eliminate systematic risk. Understanding risk is one of the most important parts of investing. question: This video explains how bonds pay you a return for lending out your money. When does a bond actually serve you well, and when does it not do much for you? Bonus: what's the main thing that drives bond returns up or down?
claimUnderTest: A bond is a loan you make to a government or company, which pays you interest over a set term and returns your principal at the end.
referenceAnswer:
Bonds are useful when what you need is predictability. You know the payment schedule and the maturity date in advance, so a bond can be matched against a known future expense — money for a purchase in five years can sit in something that pays along the way and returns the principal on time. That certainty also makes bonds a stabilizer in a portfolio: they don't usually fall as hard as stocks in a downturn, so a bad market year does less damage and there's something to draw on without selling stocks at a loss. For someone who'll be spending the money soon, the ceiling on returns matters much less than the floor.

Where bonds do little for you is the opposite case: a long horizon with no near-term need. The return is capped by design — you're lending, so the best case is being repaid with interest, and you get none of the upside if the borrower thrives. Over decades that gap compounds into a large difference, so a young investor loading up on bonds trades away growth for stability they don't need yet. Inflation is the other problem: a fixed payment loses purchasing power over time, so a bond yielding less than inflation loses money in real terms even though the numbers hold. Credit risk varies too — government bonds are safest, and corporate bonds pay more precisely because repayment is less certain.

Bonus: interest rates, set by the Federal Reserve. The key detail is that rates affect a bond's price, not the payments you're promised. A bond's coupon is fixed at issue, so holding to maturity means rate moves don't change what you collect. But if new bonds start paying more, yours paying the old lower rate is worth less to a buyer — so its market price falls. Rates and bond prices move in opposite directions. Credit for naming interest rates; full credit for connecting them to price.
rubric: Bonds fit when you need predictability — known payments and a known maturity date you can match to a future need
They stabilize a portfolio, falling less than stocks in a downturn so you're not forced to sell shares at a bad time
The return is capped: you're a lender, so you get interest and principal but none of the upside of ownership
Over a long horizon that cap costs you real growth, and inflation can erode a fixed payment's purchasing power
